Action Plan:
1. Prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid cream (name and dose/route/frequency not documented) for affected areas of chest, hands, and inner elbows for 7–10 days, then reassess efficacy.  
2. Prescribe an emollient/bath/shower moisturizer and instruct patient to use it regularly (at every wash) for the next 7–10 days.  
3. Prescribe a non-sedating oral antihistamine (Fexofenadine; dose/frequency not documented) to reduce pruritus.  
4. Advise patient to keep a diary of possible triggers (e.g., soaps, detergents, fabrics) and avoid identified irritants/allergens.  
5. Arrange follow-up: patient to return in 1 week if symptoms have not improved or sooner if rash worsens or signs of infection develop.  
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: 4-day history of intensely itchy, red, sore skin rash.  
• Location: chest, hands, inner elbows; no face or legs involvement.  
• Characteristics: very pruritic, dry, “cracked,” interferes with sleep and work; showers give transient relief. No bleeding, discharge, or pus.  
• No associated fever, systemic symptoms, respiratory, urinary, or bowel issues.  
• Past medical history: atopic eczema (previously limited to arms); childhood asthma (resolved).  
• Medications tried: OTC topical steroid cream, OTC antihistamines (names/doses not provided) – minimal relief.  
• Regular medications: none.  
• Allergies: none known.  
• Social history: 31-year-old male; lives with flatmates; project manager at pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; drinks a few beers per week; enjoys hiking.

Objective:
• Video examination (limited audio quality): diffuse erythematous, dry, cracked rash over chest, hands, and inner elbows; no visible exudate, vesicles, burrows, or bleeding noted.  
• Vitals: not recorded.  
• No other system findings documented.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Generalised pruritic rash / suspected eczema flare:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare (supported by DDx: “Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare” – High likelihood).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis (DDx – Medium) – acute onset, distribution includes hands/chest; no clear exposure identified.  
     • Scabies infestation (DDx – Medium-Low) – severe pruritus, hand involvement, shared living; no burrows or contact symptoms reported.  
     • Acute urticaria (DDx – Low) – less consistent with dry/cracked lesions.  
   - Investigations: None planned at this stage; clinical diagnosis.  
   - Treatment:  
     • Prescription-strength topical corticosteroid cream (stronger than OTC preparation).  
     • Regular emollient use (bath/shower additive and moisturizer).  
     • Oral antihistamine (Fexofenadine) for itch relief.  
   - Referrals: None now; consider dermatology referral if poor response to treatment or diagnosis unclear on follow-up.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected: objective vitals, detailed dermatologic description (size, morphology), exact medication names/doses, vaccination status, safety-net advice regarding infection signs.  
● No internal conflicts noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: audio intermittently poor; occasional repetitions/inaudible words but core clinical content intelligible.
